title: HK$220 million in one month: customer service scams and what comes next
summary: Hong Kong's customer service impersonation fraud hit HK$220 million in August alone, more than triple the prior monthly average. Alex and Jordan also work through the HKMA annual self-assessment deadline, overdue STR quality findings, and what the 11 Skies ownership transfer means for beneficial ownership transparency.
script:
ALEX: The number that stopped me this morning is HK$220 million. That is what Hongkongers lost to customer service impersonation scams in August 2026 alone. The Hong Kong Police Force published that figure, and it is more than triple the monthly average recorded across the first seven months of the year. Jordan, before we get into the mechanics, I want to know whether you think that spike changes anything for supervised institutions, or whether this is a law enforcement story that compliance teams can watch from a distance.

JORDAN: It is absolutely not a watch-from-a-distance story, and I will tell you exactly why. A customer service impersonation fraud at that volume does not stay invisible in the banking system. Victims are moving money. Mule accounts are receiving it. Transaction monitoring teams should be seeing the signals, and if they are not, that is a control question, not a police question.

ALEX: That is a fair challenge, and I take it. But I do want to push on one thing. The police figures cover gross losses to victims. We do not have a clean read yet on how much of that flowed through bank accounts versus stored-value facilities or peer-to-peer platforms. The typology matters for where you deploy the detection effort.

JORDAN: It matters, but not in the way you are suggesting. The mule account is the mule account whether the victim initiated the transfer from a bank or a stored-value facility. If you are an authorised institution under the HKMA's AML and CFT guideline, you are responsible for the account on the receiving end of the fraud flow. That is where the suspicious transaction report obligation bites.

ALEX: Agreed on that. So what is the practical read for listeners?

JORDAN: The practical read is this. If your transaction monitoring team has not reviewed its mule account detection scenarios in the last quarter, now is the time. Specifically, look at whether your rules are calibrated to catch small-value rapid-succession inflows from multiple retail originators. That is the pattern customer service scams generate. The inflows are often individually below your alert threshold, but the velocity and the originator scatter are the tell. Convene your financial crime operations team this week and pull the August and September alert data against that typology.

ALEX: And I would add a governance layer for MLROs. If your STR volumes for mule accounts did not move upward in August, you need to be able to explain to your examiner why. Because the HKMA will ask.

JORDAN: Which leads us neatly to the HKMA self-assessment, because the deadline for the annual AML and CFT self-assessment return was the thirtieth of September. That was four days ago.

ALEX: Right. And for anyone who has not submitted, the submission window has closed. The return covers customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, STR filing, training, governance, and independent audit, all under section 11 of the HKMA AML and CFT guideline. If you are in that position, your immediate call is to your HKMA relationship supervisor, not an internal working group.

JORDAN: I want to add something, though, because I think some listeners will be in a slightly different position. They filed on time, but they filed something they were not fully satisfied with. Maybe the independent audit finding was still open. Maybe the ongoing monitoring section was thin on evidence. The self-assessment is not just a form. It is the document your examiner will read before the next supervisory visit. If you know there are gaps in what you filed, document the gap and your remediation plan internally now, before you are asked.

ALEX: Which connects directly to the still-open item from the HKMA's Q4 2025 thematic review of STR narrative quality. Deficiency letters went to roughly a quarter of the supervised institution population. Closure of those findings is overdue. For any institution that received one of those letters, the HKMA expects documented evidence of remediation, not just a policy update. We are talking about revised narrative templates, training records, and a sample review showing the new quality standard is being applied consistently.

JORDAN: And I will be direct. If you are an MLRO at a named institution and that closure has been sitting with your legal or governance team for sign-off, move it this week. An open thematic finding at the same time as a late or thin self-assessment return is not a combination you want to explain at a supervisory meeting.

ALEX: Shifting focus slightly, there is a story out of Hong Kong that is getting coverage primarily as a property and infrastructure story, but I think it deserves a moment here. The Hong Kong Airport Authority is taking over the 11 Skies commercial development from New World Development, with the transfer expected in April 2027. This is a large-scale project moving from a listed private developer into public hands. The question I am sitting with is what happens to the beneficial ownership records compiled during the private development phase.

JORDAN: I see why you flagged it, but I think the compliance risk is narrower than you are framing it. The Airport Authority itself is a statutory body. The ownership transparency concern is not at the Authority level. It is at the level of any private joint venture partners, contractors, or tenants who remain in the structure post-transfer. Those are the relationships that need fresh customer due diligence if you are a bank financing any part of this.

ALEX: That is a sharper read. So for banks with exposure to the project's financing or to the contractor network, the April 2027 transfer date is a triggering event for ownership re-verification, even if the underlying counterparty has not changed.

JORDAN: Exactly. Put it in your diary now as a CDD refresh trigger. Do not wait for the transfer to complete.

ALEX: Before we close, a quick note for Singapore-based listeners. The MAS Notice 626 quarterly STR governance review for the quarter ending September was due in July. If your institution runs the review on a calendar quarter lag, you should be in the middle of that process right now. Completeness, timeliness, escalation effectiveness, and reconciliation against STRO acknowledgements. That is the scope. Do not let it slip into November.

JORDAN: And one more for the Australians. The annual AML and CTF Program review under section 84 of the AML and CTF Act was due at the end of August. If your board has not formally approved the updated program, that is a high-priority item for your next board or board risk committee meeting. The approval needs to be minuted.

ALEX: The full obligation register with source links is at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. If today's episode surfaced a deadline you had not tracked, that is where to check what else is in the pipeline.

JORDAN: The through-line across everything today is that the third quarter just closed and the fourth quarter review cycle is opening. Regulators in Hong Kong and Singapore are looking at what you filed, what you said you would do, and whether the evidence matches. If any of that felt uncomfortably close to home, that is the point. See you tomorrow.
